```{r, echo = FALSE, message = FALSE}
library(knitr)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
    error = FALSE,
    tidy  = FALSE,
    warning = FALSE,
    message = FALSE,
    comment = NA,
    fig.align = "center")
library(argitect)

options(cli.num_colors = 1)

run_code = function(code_block, argv_str) {
    chunks = knitr:::knit_code$get()
    argitect_options("__argv_str__" = argv_str)
    local({ 
        for(cb in code_block)
            eval(parse(text = chunks[[cb]])) 
    })
    argitect_options(RESET = TRUE)
}
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## A quick example

When a script gets complicated, it might be better to split it into several
sub-scripts where each is focused on a specific task. Here `sub_commands()` 
supports to dispatch command-line options to sub-scripts.

The following code gives you a quick example of how the sub commands are set.
In the function `sub_commands()`, the name of the sub-command, the sub-script and the 
description of the sub-command are organized as a 3-tuple.

The following code is put in the script called `main.R` (parent script) which
contains dispatches of sub-commands.

```{r main, eval = FALSE}
library(argitect)

sub_commands(
    "sub1", "sub1.R", "Description of sub command 1.",
    "sub2", "sub2.R", "Description of sub command 2."
)
```

Code in `sub1.R`:

```{r sub1, eval = FALSE}
library(argitect)

argitect("foo=i", "Set value for foo.")

cat("foo is ", foo, "\n")
```

And code in `sub2.R`:

```{r sub2, eval = FALSE}
library(argitect)

argitect("bar=i", "Set value for bar")

cat("bar is ", bar, "\n")
```

Calling `main.R` with no argument prints the list of sub-commands it supports.

```
~\> Rscript main.R
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE}
run_code("main", "")
```

When a sub-command is called, the corresponding R script is invoked. Here all
command-line arguments after the sub command `sub1` go to the correspond R
script `sub1.R`. Internally, it actually executes `Rscript sub1.R --help`.

```
~\> Rscript main.R sub1 --help
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE}
run_code("main", "sub1 --help")
```

Options in `sub1.R` can be directly set after the sub-command, which internally
equivalent to `Rscript sub1.R --foo 10`.

```
~\> Rscript main.R sub1 --foo 10
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE}
run_code("main", "sub1 --foo 10")
```

A [shebang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shebang_(Unix)) line can be added to
the first line of the parent R script, then `Rscript` is not necessary to be explicitely called.
Also `.R` suffix of the parent script can be removed to pretend it is a linux utility program.

```r
#!/usr/bin/env Rscript
library(argitect)

sub_commands(
    "sub1", "sub1.R", "This is sub-command 1.",
    "sub2", "sub2.R", "This is sub-command 2."
)
```

Make sure `main` is executable.

```
./main sub1 --foo 1
```

If the directory of script `main` is put into `PATH` and all sub-command
scripts are accessible from `main`, then 

```
main sub1 --foo 1
```


## The specification

Besides the 3-tuple specification demonstrated already, sub-commands can also
be specified in 2-tuples, where the first element is the sub-script and the
second element is the description of the sub-command. In this scenario, the basename
of the sub-script removing `.R`/`.r` suffix is taken as the name of the sub-command.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
sub_commands(
    "sub1.R", "This is sub-command 1.",
    "sub2.R", "This is sub-command 2."
)
```

With 3-tuple specification, names of the sub-commands can be self-defined.

```{r 3-tuple, eval = FALSE}
sub_commands(
    "one", "sub1.R", "This is sub-command 1.",
    "two", "sub2.R", "This is sub-command 2."
)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE}
run_code("3-tuple", "")
```

As all parameters are specified as a long vector in `sub_commands()`, whether
it is a 3-tuple format or a 2-tuple format is automatically determined.

## Sections

A separator line (a name consisting only of `-`, `=`, `+`, `#` or `%`) starts
a new section, just like in `argitect()`. The section title is the
corresponding description. With the 3-tuple form:

```{r section-3-tuple, eval = FALSE}
sub_commands(
    "----", "----", "Section one",
    "sub1", "sub1.R", "This is sub-command 1.",

    "----", "----", "Section two",
    "sub2", "sub2.R", "This is sub-command 2."
)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE}
run_code("section-3-tuple", "")
```

And with the 2-tuple form:

```{r section-2-tuple, eval = FALSE}
sub_commands(
    "----", "Section one",
    "sub1.R", "This is sub-command 1.",

    "----", "Section two",
    "sub2.R", "This is sub-command 2."
)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE}
run_code("section-2-tuple", "")
```


## Setting help head and foot

`help_head` adds text before the help message and `help_foot` adds text after the help message.


```{r head-foot, eval = FALSE}
sub_commands(
    help_head = "This is the head of the help message.",

    "sub1", "sub1.R", "This is sub-command 1.",
    "sub2", "sub2.R", "This is sub-command 2.",

    help_foot = "This is the foot of the help message."
)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE}
run_code("head-foot", "")
```


## Template

A single string is treated as a template, where each command is marked by the
`template_tag` (default `<CODE>`). The code part can be either `script.R`
(the command name is derived from the file name) or `command=script.R`:

```{r template1, eval = FALSE}
sub_commands(
"This is the head of the help message.

Usage: Rscript main.R [command] [options]

Commands:
  <sub1.R> This is sub-command 1.
  <sub2=sub2.R> This is sub-command 2.

This is the foot of the help message.
")
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE}
run_code("template1", "")
```

The same as in `argitect()`, here the template also allows `{{...}}` to contain executable code to interpolate
and to insert into the template.

```{r template2, eval = FALSE}
sub1_script = system.file("extdata", "sub1.R", package = "argitect")
sub2_script = system.file("extdata", "sub2.R", package = "argitect")
sub_commands(
"This is the head of the help message.

Usage: Rscript main.R [command] [options]

{{ cli_h2('Section') }}
  <sub1={{ sub1_script }}> This is sub-command 1.
  <sub2={{ sub2_script }}> This is sub-command 2.

This is the foot of the help message.

Questions, please contact {{ col_magenta(style_underline(style_italic('your.name@email'))) }}
")
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE}
run_code("template2", "")
```

## –-help and –-version

`--help` on the parent script is the same as giving no argument, which prints
the list of sub-commands. `--version` prints the `VERSION` variable from the
calling environment. Both `-h` and `-v` are accepted as well.

```{r version, eval = FALSE}
VERSION = "1.0.0"
sub_commands(
    "sub1.R", "This is sub command 1.",
    "sub2.R", "This is sub command 2."
)
```

```
~\> Rscript main.R --version
1.0.0
```

## Script existence

The sub-scripts must exist. If a specified sub-script path does not exist,
`sub_commands()` raises an error:

```{r, error = TRUE}
sub_commands(
    "sub1", "non_existing_dir/sub1.R", "This is sub command 1."
)
```
